short_description: A Bayesian statistics monograph built on de Finetti, Sanov and Bayes: exchangeable prediction under moment constraints gives maximum entropy laws, and testing, shrinkage, asymptotics and decision are read on one moderate deviation scale.
description:
Bayesian inference is a predictive act. This book builds it from three ideas: de Finetti supplies the structure, writing exchangeable beliefs as mixtures of independent laws; Sanov supplies the asymptotics, the exponential concentration of empirical measures at a rate given by the Kullback Leibler divergence; and Bayes supplies the updating, an exponential tilt of the predictive law. Together they give a tilted de Finetti theorem: conditioning an exchangeable sequence on empirical moment constraints yields predictive laws that are I projections of a baseline measure, so parameters emerge as limits of empirical functionals and maximum entropy appears as a predictive limit rather than a postulate. Testing, shrinkage, asymptotics and decision are then read on one moderate deviation scale.

Results the book proves, most first stated in the authors' papers with Daniel Zantedeschi and Jyotishka Datta: a finite sample total variation bound between a block drawn under a moment window and independent draws from the I projection, and the projected de Finetti limit behind it; a split of the predictive Kullback Leibler Bayes risk into a Sanov term and a posterior contraction term,; a condition for a scalar learning rate to calibrate credible sets at moderate scale, namely that model curvature and score covariance be proportional; one control variate form for Bayes linear and prediction powered inference estimators, with the optimal gain in closed form; the global posterior of federated learning as a product of local experts under exchangeability; and a convergence rate for the policy that maximizes posterior expected utility in generative Bayesian computation. Several results are stated conditionally or as open problems, and the book says which.

Later chapters treat computation, universal portfolios, causal machine learning and medicine. Scripts reproducing every computed figure and number are in the repository.

chapters.title: Prediction, Exchangeability, and the Predictive Paradigm
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks what the primitive object of statistical inference is and answers that it is the predictive distribution of the next observation, with the parameter and prior as derived devices. It develops exchangeability and de Finetti's representation theorem, with a complete proof for binary sequences by the urn argument of Heath and Sudderth, whose coupling error for a block of m variables is m(m minus 1)/(2N), and the Hewitt and Savage extension through the directing measure. It previews Sanov's theorem with its I projection and the inverse Sanov theorem of Ganesh and O'Connell for posterior concentration. It then reads modern machine learning as Bayesian prediction: conformal prediction, in context learning of large language models, diffusion and score based generators, and amortized simulation based inference, each a device that manufactures a predictive rule, with martingale posteriors, calibration and coverage, and a translation table.

#### From the literature

- De Finetti's theorem for exchangeable sequences (de Finetti 1937), with the proof for binary sequences by Heath and Sudderth (1976).
- The Hewitt and Savage extension to general spaces (Hewitt and Savage 1955).
- Sanov's theorem (Sanov 1957), stated here as a preview.
- The inverse Sanov theorem (Ganesh and O'Connell 1999, 2000), stated here as a preview.
- Martingale posteriors (Fong, Holmes and Walker 2023), conformal prediction (Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer 2005) and the Bayesian bootstrap (Rubin 1981), presented as predictive devices.

#### New results

The chapter's theorems are known results presented as previews; its contribution, the predictive framing and the reading of machine learning methods, is not a catalogued theorem.

No new results of this chapter are catalogued.

chapters.title: Information, Types, and Large Deviations
chapters.summary:
This chapter builds the information theoretic engine: the method of types, which bounds the probability of a type by exp of minus N D(Q||P) up to a polynomial factor; entropy, relative entropy (Kullback Leibler divergence) and mutual information; Stirling bounds and the equipartition property; and the Heath and Sudderth proof of de Finetti's theorem as the method of types on a scalar lattice. It proves Sanov's theorem for a positive law on a finite alphabet and a closed convex set of laws equal to the closure of its interior, through the dominant type, with the I projection and the divergence gap, and states the conditional limit theorem (Gibbs conditioning principle) of van Campenhout and Cover and Csiszar. It covers exponential families and maximum entropy, Cramer's theorem and the Legendre transform, Stein's lemma and Chernoff information, the three deviation scales, equivalence of ensembles, and the case for relative entropy among divergences.

#### From the literature

- The method of types, in its standard form for finite alphabets.
- De Finetti's theorem for binary sequences, by the Heath and Sudderth (1976) argument on a type lattice.
- Sanov's theorem (Sanov 1957) and the I projection (Csiszar 1975, 1984).
- The conditional limit theorem and Gibbs conditioning (van Campenhout and Cover 1981; Csiszar 1984).
- Cramer's theorem, Stein's lemma and Chernoff information, and the maximum entropy principle (Jaynes 1957).

#### New results

This chapter fixes notation and presents known results; its recasting of Heath and Sudderth as the method of types on a scalar lattice is exposition of a classical theorem.

No new results of this chapter are catalogued.

chapters.title: The Tilted de Finetti Synthesis
chapters.summary:
This chapter proves the book's central result, the tilted de Finetti theorem: conditioning an exchangeable sequence on an empirical moment constraint yields predictive laws that are exponential family I projections of the directing measure. For a finite alphabet, a polyhedral moment window, an interior I projection and strong regularity, a split set master inequality bounds the total variation distance between a constrained block of m coordinates and the product of the I projection, with tuned rate O(m eps_N + m sqrt(log N / N) + m^2/N). Mixing over the constraint posterior gives the projected de Finetti limit, its predictive corollary, and a classification of reachable, null and unreachable constraints, with the null constraint trap. The posterior is a Gibbs measure (inverse Sanov), with the Ganesh and O'Connell large deviation principle and the curvature identity linking Fisher information to the rate function. It closes with Diaconis's finite de Finetti theorem, conditional limits and conjugate priors.

#### From the literature

- The inverse Sanov theorem for posteriors (Ganesh and O'Connell 1999, 2000), with the exponential family case of Macci and Piccioni (2023).
- Gibbs conditioning (van Campenhout and Cover 1981; Csiszar 1984).
- The finite de Finetti theorem (Diaconis and Freedman 1980a) and the conditional limit theorem for exponential families (Diaconis and Freedman 1988).
- The characterization of conjugate priors for exponential families (Diaconis and Ylvisaker 1979).
- Links between maximum entropy and Bayes (Jaynes 1957; Dinwoodie and Zabell 1992; Fortini, Ladelli and Regazzini 2000) and PAC Bayes bounds (Catoni 2007).

#### New results

These results come from the authors' paper De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes and are stated for a finite alphabet.

- [Componentwise constrained horizon master inequality](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#constrained_horizon_master_inequality) (Theorem 3.2, page 30; proved): A fixed block of coordinates drawn from a sample conditioned on a moment window is close in total variation to independent draws from the I projection, with an explicit finite sample bound with three separately controlled terms. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).
- [Tuned rate for the constrained block law](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#master_inequality_tuning) (Corollary 3.3, page 30; proved): Choosing the split radius of order the square root of log N over N gives a block law rate of order m eps_N plus m sqrt(log N / N) plus m squared over N. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).
- [Projected de Finetti limit](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#projected_de_finetti_limit) (Theorem 3.4, page 32; proved): After mixing over the constraint posterior, the block laws of an exchangeable sequence conditioned on a moment event converge to an exchangeable law whose random directing measure is the I projection of the original directing measure. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).
- [Bayesian prediction under the constrained limit](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#bayesian_prediction_under_constrained_limit) (Corollary 3.5, page 33; proved): Under the projected de Finetti limit, the predictive probability of the next observation is the usual de Finetti posterior predictive under the prior induced by the I projection map. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).
- [Reachability and degeneracy of moment constraints](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#reachability_and_degeneracy) (Proposition 3.7, page 34; conditional on proofs of its four clauses, which the book states without proof, in particular the concentration rate max(eps_N, N^{-1/2}) and the disintegration limit in clause (ii) and the transverse dimension k-1-r_0 in clause (iv)): Whether a moment constraint is reachable by the prior decides whether the I projection acts, with reachable constraints truncating or disintegrating the prior, unreachable ones leaving genuine tilts, and affine constraints able to collapse the randomness; the book states this without proof. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).

chapters.title: Risk, Coding, and Shrinkage
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks what a Bayesian decision costs, what the shortest description of data is, and how a sparse high dimensional signal should be shrunk, and answers on the moderate deviation scale, square root of log n. It treats Bayes risk and risk optimal testing thresholds for genome wide screening; nonparametric predictive Bayes risk, which splits the Kullback Leibler risk of a posterior predictive density into a Sanov term (the reverse I projection of the truth on the prior support) and a posterior contraction term, with Kolmogorov Smirnov thresholds and adaptive rates for Dirichlet process mixtures, Polya trees and logistic Gaussian processes; minimum description length, Bayesian evidence and singular BIC; Kolmogorov complexity; James Stein and global local shrinkage; and the horseshoe prior, its log pole, super efficiency and asymptotic Bayes optimality under sparsity (ABOS). The three nonparametric rates are conditional on a stated assumption, and the optimal Kolmogorov Smirnov truncation level, a moderate deviation threshold for non regular Ibragimov and Has'minskii models, and ABOS of the horseshoe and the beta horseshoe under exponential power noise are conjectures.

Rubin and Sethuraman (1965a, 1965b) on moderate deviations and Bayes risk efficiency; Aitchison (1975) and Clarke and Barron (1990) on predictive risk; Csiszar (1975) on I projection; Kleijn and van der Vaart (2006, 2012) on misspecified posteriors; Smirnov (1944) on the Kolmogorov Smirnov tail; Lavine (1992), Escobar and West (1995), Castillo (2017) and van der Vaart and van Zanten (2009) on nonparametric priors; Rissanen (1978) and MacKay (1992) on description length and evidence; Kolmogorov (1965), Chaitin (1966) and Solomonoff (1964) on algorithmic complexity; Stein (1956) and James and Stein (1961) on shrinkage; Carvalho, Polson and Scott (2010) and Polson and Scott (2010) on the horseshoe; Bogdan, Chakrabarti, Frommlet and Ghosh (2011) and Datta and Ghosh (2013) on ABOS; Ibragimov and Has'minskii (1981) on non regular models.

The chapter proves the predictive Bayes risk decomposition and the moderate deviation risk balancing thresholds; the tilted de Finetti limit (Polson and Zantedeschi 2025a) and the normal mean testing boundary (Datta, Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi 2026) are quoted without proof.

- [Decomposition of nonparametric predictive Bayes risk into Sanov and contraction terms](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#predictive_bayes_risk_decomposition) (Theorem 4.1, page 59; proved): The predictive KL Bayes risk splits into a population Sanov term, a posterior contraction term and a small cross term, so misspecified models have risk equal to the Sanov term and well specified ones have risk equal to the contraction term. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026i), Nonparametric Predictive Bayes Risk, working paper.
- [Conditional Sanov and tilted de Finetti](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#conditional_sanov_tilted_de_finetti) (Theorem 4.5, page 61; proved): Conditioned on the empirical measure lying in a closed convex set, the predictive law of a fixed block converges to the I projection of the de Finetti baseline onto that set. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).
- [Bayes risk optimal Kolmogorov Smirnov threshold at the moderate deviation scale](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#rubin_sethuraman_risk_balancing_ks) (Theorem 4.9, page 65; proved): The Bayes risk optimal Kolmogorov Smirnov threshold sits at about half the detection distance, with the exact constant 3/8 and risk of order n to the minus 25/16 at the boundary Delta_n = sqrt(2 log n) with prior odds n. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026b), Bayes Risk for Goodness of Fit Tests.
- [General moderate deviation risk balancing threshold for tests](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#rubin_sethuraman_risk_balancing_general) (Theorem 4.11, page 68; proved): For any statistic with Gaussian type moderate deviation tails under null and alternative, the Bayes risk optimal threshold is half the detection scale plus a prior odds correction, and it is at least the multiple comparison scale sqrt(2 log b_n). First stated in Datta, Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026), A New Look at Bayesian Testing.
- [Optimal truncation at the moderate deviation scale](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#optimal_truncation_moderate_deviation_scale) (Conjecture 4.15, page 72; open): The book conjectures that the Bayes risk optimal truncation level for a Kolmogorov Smirnov truncated predictive density equals the detection distance, which is sqrt(2 log n) at the detection boundary, and gives a heuristic only. chapters.title: Predictive Geometry and Maximum Entropy
chapters.summary:
What does conditioning on information do to a predictive distribution, and how are the resulting projections computed? This chapter treats moment conditioning as projection onto an affine family, with relative entropy as squared distance and a Pythagorean theorem. Conditioning an independent sample from a reference law on its empirical moments gives an exact mixture over empirical types. On the constraint chart the mixing law is asymptotically Gaussian with precision given by a reduced Hessian, and a fixed block of draws collapses to independent draws from the I projection (the exponential tilt), with explicit total variation bounds for exactly feasible and generic windowed constraints. Parameterizing the projected family gives a predictive product criterion that is locally a generalized method of moments objective, related to exponentially tilted empirical likelihood. The second half treats maximum entropy algorithms as one master routine, alternating minimization, with iterative proportional fitting and iterative scaling, Dykstra and Bregman projection, Blahut and Arimoto, and majorization as its faces, and shows that the Gibbs rule is an entropic proximal operator. It also gives a counterexample showing that the mutual information Hessian in a channel parameter need not be positive semidefinite.

#### From the literature

The I projection theorem, Pythagorean identity and Gibbs form of the minimizer (Csiszar 1975). Sanov's theorem and the conditional limit theorem (Sanov 1957; van Campenhout and Cover 1981; Csiszar 1984). Alternating minimization, the five point property and convergence (Csiszar and Tusnady 1984). Cyclic I projection onto affine sets and generalized iterative scaling (Csiszar 1975; Darroch and Ratcliff 1972). Dykstra's algorithm (Dykstra 1985; Censor and Reich 1998). Blahut and Arimoto algorithms (Blahut 1972; Arimoto 1972). Empirical likelihood, exponentially tilted empirical likelihood and efficient generalized method of moments (Owen 1988, 2001; Qin and Lawless 1994; Schennach 2005).

#### New results

The chapter's new results are the collapse, localization and moment criterion theorems of the moment conditioning section (Polson and Zantedeschi 2025b), which depend on supplementary proofs, and the counterexample on the mutual information Hessian (2026d).

- [Gaussian localization on the constraint chart](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#gaussian_localization_constraint_chart) (Theorem 5.8, page 155; conditional on the bad type suppression and good type Gaussian control lemmas and the fixed chart Taylor, Stirling and coarea remainder constants, which the book states with outline proofs only and defers to the Supplementary Material of the source paper): The conditioned predictive law of a block is a Gaussian mixture of product laws centered at the I projection, with precision given by the reduced Hessian. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025b), Bayesian Prediction under Moment Conditioning.
- [Exchangeable block collapse under moment conditioning](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#exchangeable_block_collapse) (Theorem 5.10, page 156; conditional on the Gaussian localization theorem on the constraint chart, whose proof the book only outlines, deferring the bad type suppression and good type Gaussian control lemmas and the fixed chart remainder constants to the Supplementary Material of the source paper; the step from localization to the collapse bound is proved in the book): Conditioning an independent sample on its empirical moments makes any fixed block of draws asymptotically independent from the I projection, with an explicit total variation bound in the block size and the reduced Hessian. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025b), Bayesian Prediction under Moment Conditioning.
- [Window robust collapse without lattice regularity](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#window_robust_collapse) (Theorem 5.11, page 156; conditional on the conditional concentration of the empirical cell frequencies around the slab minimizer at rate the square root of log n over n, and the distance of order the tolerance between the slab minimizer and the I projection, both cited in the book's outline proof from the Supplementary Material of the source paper): For generic real valued moments, where exact feasibility fails, conditioning on a shrinking tolerance window still makes a fixed block asymptotically independent from the I projection, with a coarser rate. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025b), Bayesian Prediction under Moment Conditioning.
- [Lifted collapse to the ambient predictive law under refinement](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#lifted_diagonal_collapse) (Corollary 5.15, page 159; conditional on the projection approximation lemma (Lemma S3 of the Supplementary Material of the source paper), which bounds the total variation between the lifted chart projection and the ambient I projection by the cell oscillation, and the window robust collapse bound): Letting the partition refine slowly with the sample size, the conditioned block law lifted back to the sample space converges to independent draws from the ambient I projection. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025b), Bayesian Prediction under Moment Conditioning.
- [Projection induced moment criterion is a generalized method of moments](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#projection_induced_moment_criterion) (Proposition 5.20, page 163; conditional on the dual expansion proof in the Supplementary Material of the source paper, which the book does not reproduce): The negative log of the induced conditional likelihood is locally a quadratic form in the moment residuals weighted by the inverse cell moment covariance, as in efficient generalized method of moments. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025b), Bayesian Prediction under Moment Conditioning.
- [Mutual information Hessian in the channel parameter need not be positive semidefinite](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#mutual_information_hessian_not_psd) (Proposition 5.33, page 188; counterexample, proved): The second derivative of mutual information with respect to a softmax channel parameter can be negative, so a published identification diagnostic that treats it as positive semidefinite is not valid. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026d), Maximum Entropy Algorithms for Predictive Rules: Blahut-Arimoto, Conditional Limits, and Iterative Scaling, working paper.

chapters.title: Bayes, E-values, and Testing
chapters.summary:
A test is a decision taken on evidence, and this chapter separates three questions that are often run together: what the evidence is, why acting on it controls error, and where to draw the line. The evidence is the likelihood ratio, canonical under logarithmic loss, an e variable and e process whose validity comes from the supermartingale property and Ville's inequality at every stopping time. The line is drawn by a Bayes risk calculation on the moderate deviation scale: the Bayes boundary for a point null rejects when the squared standardized statistic exceeds (dimension plus prior order) times log n, between the central limit scale of fixed critical values and the large deviation scale of fixed alternatives. The chapter states the moderate deviation principle and derives the fixed sample threshold and the sequential stopping time, with Gaussian fluctuations on the square root of log b scale. It gives the risk optimal Bayes factor threshold and the Rubin and Sethuraman analysis of the boundary, the order of the minimal Bayes risk, and Bayes risk efficiency compared with Pitman and Bahadur efficiency.

#### From the literature

Ville's inequality for nonnegative supermartingales (Ville 1939). E variables, e processes and anytime valid inference (Ramdas, Ruf, Larsson and Koolen 2022). The numeraire e variable (Larsson, Ramdas and Ruf 2025). Martingale posteriors (Fong, Holmes and Walker 2023). Minimax regret and the normalized maximum likelihood code (Shtarkov 1987). Wald's identity and sequential testing (Wald 1947; Siegmund 1985); Lorden's overshoot bound (Lorden 1970). Moderate deviation probabilities (Rubin and Sethuraman 1965a), proved by the Gartner and Ellis argument. Jeffreys' testing threshold (Jeffreys 1961) and Lindley's paradox (Lindley 1957). The Rubin and Sethuraman Bayes risk boundary, the order of the minimal Bayes risk, and Bayes risk efficiency, which agrees with Pitman efficiency (Rubin and Sethuraman 1965a, 1965b). Pitman efficiency (Pitman 1948); Bahadur efficiency (Bahadur 1960).

#### New results

The new results are the canonical sequential evidence theorem with its liftability, normalized maximum likelihood tradeoff and log loss companions, and the risk optimal Bayes factor threshold.

- [Likelihood ratio is the canonical sequential evidence under log loss](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#canonical_sequential_evidence) (Theorem 6.1, page 195; proved): The Bayes test rejects when the prior predictive likelihood ratio exceeds a cost determined threshold, and that ratio is an e variable and the unique maximizer of expected log growth among e variables. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026a), Bayes, E-values, and Testing.
- [Sequential liftability of a codelength to an e process](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#sequential_liftability_codelength) (Theorem 6.3, page 197; proved): A codelength gives an e process exactly when its one step factors form a sub probability kernel, which fails for normalized maximum likelihood codes at changing horizons. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026a), Bayes, E-values, and Testing.
- [Complexity validity tradeoff between minimax regret codes and e processes](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#complexity_validity_tradeoff) (Corollary 6.4, page 198; proved): No code that attains the minimax individual sequence regret at every horizon gives an e process unless the normalized maximum likelihood laws of successive horizons are consistent. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026a), Bayes, E-values, and Testing.
- [Log loss is the unique scoring rule giving a martingale evidence process](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#log_loss_uniqueness_evidence) (Proposition 6.5, page 198; proved): Among strictly proper scoring rules only the log score yields an evidence process that is a null martingale for every alternative, and other rules grow no faster than the log loss rate. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026a), Bayes, E-values, and Testing.
- [Risk optimal Bayes factor threshold on the moderate deviation band](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#risk_optimal_bayes_factor_threshold) (Theorem 6.9, page 210; proved): For a normal mean and a point null, the Bayes factor and the risk optimal rejection cutoff, whose leading term log n is Jeffreys' threshold, hold with a uniform remainder on the moderate deviation band, with constants set by the prior density at the null, the variance and the prior odds. First stated in Datta, Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026), A New Look at Bayesian Testing.

chapters.title: Posterior Asymptotics and the Gaussian Regime
chapters.summary:
Why is the posterior so often approximately Gaussian, and when is it not? The chapter studies posterior asymptotics: Bernstein and von Mises theorems, posterior consistency and contraction rates, merging of opinions, martingale structure of marginal likelihoods and Bayes factors, and the Gaussian regime read off the curvature of the Kullback Leibler rate function. It treats the posterior as obeying a large deviation principle (a Bayesian Sanov theorem, reverse information projection) whose Hessian at the truth is the Fisher information, and adds the moderate deviation scale between the central limit and large deviation scales, with non coverage exponents of credible sets. It covers misspecified models (Kullback Leibler projection, sandwich covariance, Bartlett identity, Gibbs and tempered posteriors, learning rate calibration), mean field variational anti conservatism, dependent data with long run variance, proportional asymptotics for high dimensional regression, and failures of Bernstein and von Mises (mixed normality, non regular models, mixtures). It closes with a critique of martingale posteriors and the classes of Blackwell admissible, anytime valid and conformal rules.

#### From the literature

Blackwell and Dubins merging of opinions (1962); Doob consistency (Doob 1949); the Bernstein and von Mises theorem; Berk's misspecified posterior concentration (1966); the Ghosal, Ghosh and van der Vaart contraction rate theorem (2000); the Kleijn and van der Vaart misspecified Bernstein and von Mises theorem (2012); posterior mixed normality after Heyde and Johnstone (1979); moderate deviations for the posterior (Eichelsbacher and Ganesh 2002); the conditional limit theorem (Csiszar 1984; Cover and Thomas 2006); Bissiri, Holmes and Walker Gibbs posteriors (2016); the complete class theorem of Wald and Le Cam; martingale posteriors of Fong, Holmes and Walker (2023); the inverse Sanov theorem (Ganesh and O'Connell 1999); the sandwich covariance under misspecification (White 1982; Muller 2013).

#### New results

The new statements are the Bayesian Sanov principle under misspecification, the non coverage exponents and three regimes results on moderate scales, the calibration results for tempered and variational posteriors under misspecification and dependence, the functional Bernstein and von Mises theorem at proportional dimension, and the moment gap and admissibility separation results for martingale posteriors.

- [Moment gap of martingale posteriors](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#moment_gap_martingale_posterior) (Proposition 7.8, page 238; proved): A martingale of posterior means does not determine the k step run probability from the current value alone, although the whole path of values does. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026a), Martingale Posterior Predictive Coherence: Hausdorff Moment Hierarchy.
- [Predictive variance gap for martingale posteriors](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#predictive_variance_gap) (Corollary 7.9, page 238; proved): Under the martingale posterior condition the current value does not determine the predictive variance or the coverage of a prediction set for the next k observations when k is at least 2. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026a), Martingale Posterior Predictive Coherence: Hausdorff Moment Hierarchy.
- [Blackwell admissible, anytime valid and conformal rules are non nested](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#admissibility_classes_non_nested) (Proposition 7.11, page 242; proved): The classes of Blackwell admissible, anytime valid admissible and conformal valid rules are pairwise non nested, and the martingale condition is necessary for the first but does not characterize any of them. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026b), Bayes with No Shame: Admissibility Geometries of Predictive Inference.
- [Bayesian Sanov principle under misspecification](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#bayesian_sanov) (Proposition 7.20, page 255; proved): On a finite alphabet the posterior obeys a large deviation principle at speed n whose rate is the excess reverse relative entropy over the reverse information projection of the truth; the well specified case is the inverse Sanov theorem of Ganesh and O'Connell (1999). First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026j), Bayesian Asymptotics: Merging, Martingales, and Moderate Deviations, SSRN 7013738.
- [Non coverage exponents of credible sets on moderate scales](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#non_coverage_exponents_of_credible_sets) (Corollary 7.25, page 260; proved): On moderate scales credible balls and confidence balls have the same Gaussian tail exponent, which sharpens the Bernstein and von Mises equivalence to an exponential rate. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026j), Bayesian Asymptotics: Merging, Martingales, and Moderate Deviations, SSRN 7013738.
- [Three regimes of the posterior governed by one quadratic form](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#three_regimes_one_rate_function) (Proposition 7.26, page 261; proved): Combining the Bernstein and von Mises theorem, the moderate deviation theorem of Eichelsbacher and Ganesh and the Bayesian Sanov principle, the central limit, moderate deviation and large deviation behavior of the posterior are one rate function seen at three magnifications, with the Fisher information as its Hessian. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026j), Bayesian Asymptotics: Merging, Martingales, and Moderate Deviations, SSRN 7013738.
- [Functional Bernstein and von Mises and bulk non contraction at proportional rate](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#functional_bvm_proportional_asymptotics) (Theorem 7.30, page 271; proved): In Gaussian linear regression with dimension proportional to sample size, one dimensional functionals of the posterior are Gaussian with inflated variance and satisfy a deformed moderate deviation principle while the full posterior does not contract. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026j), Bayesian Asymptotics: Merging, Martingales, and Moderate Deviations, SSRN 7013738.
- [Moderate scale calibration of tempered posteriors under misspecification](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#moderate_scale_calibration_misspecification) (Proposition 7.31, page 272; proved): A scalar learning rate calibrates credible balls at moderate scale only when the model curvature and score covariance are proportional, and otherwise a matrix temperature is needed. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026j), Bayesian Asymptotics: Merging, Martingales, and Moderate Deviations, SSRN 7013738.
- [Best scalar temperature for a misspecified posterior](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#best_scalar_temperature) (Corollary 7.32, page 273; proved): When no scalar learning rate calibrates, the rate that matches the expected credible radius to nominal is the dimension divided by the trace of the product of inverse curvature and score covariance. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026j), Bayesian Asymptotics: Merging, Martingales, and Moderate Deviations, SSRN 7013738.
- [Moderate deviation form of mean field variational undercoverage](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#mean_field_variational_anti_conservatism) (Proposition 7.33, page 274; proved): In the Gaussian limit the product form variational approximation, whose marginal variances are classically too small, has a larger moderate deviation rate than the posterior, so its credible intervals are too narrow by a factor given by the coordinate curvature product. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026j), Bayesian Asymptotics: Merging, Martingales, and Moderate Deviations, SSRN 7013738.
- [Calibration under dependent data and the long run variance](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#dependent_data_calibration) (Proposition 7.34, page 275; conditional on the hypothesis that the posterior precision is asymptotically n V under stationary alpha mixing data and a possibly misspecified model, which the book assumes and does not derive): For mixing data the Bernstein and von Mises limit has the sandwich form with the long run score variance, and the calibrating temperature is the curvature over that variance in the scalar case. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026j), Bayesian Asymptotics: Merging, Martingales, and Moderate Deviations, SSRN 7013738.

#### Key terms

chapters.title: Scalable Computation and Deep Learning
chapters.summary:
How can the predictive theory be turned into algorithms? The chapter derives computation from the information view of prediction. It starts from an axiomatic characterization of the logarithmic score and a rate distortion frontier for entropy regularized prediction, then treats data augmentation, scale mixtures and latent variable Bayes (Polya Gamma Gibbs sampling for logistic and multinomial models), deep learning as hierarchical nonlinear regression with a coding and evidence view of regularization, and generative Bayesian prediction in which the posterior is a trained sampler built from quantile maps and noise outsourcing. It also discusses double descent, ordered empirical Bayes and the selection of complexity by evidence, and proximal algorithms with optimization as inference (penalized estimation and Langevin sampling as two readings of one iteration). It proves only a few statements of its own and mostly presents known methods in the book's predictive and maximum entropy language.

#### From the literature

Characterization of the logarithmic score (Bernardo 1979); rate distortion theory (Cover and Thomas 2006); the Polya Gamma augmentation for logistic regression (Polson, Scott and Windle 2013) and its uniform ergodicity (Choi and Hobert 2013); noise outsourcing (Kallenberg); minimum description length and evidence (Rissanen 1978; Watanabe 2009); proximal algorithms in statistics (Polson, Scott and Willard 2015); the horseshoe prior (Carvalho, Polson and Scott 2010).

#### New results

No new results of this chapter are catalogued; the log score characterization and the rate distortion frontier are presented after Bernardo (1979) and Cover and Thomas (2006).

No new results of this chapter are catalogued.

#### Key terms

chapters.title: Regularization, Nonparametric Models, and Averaging
chapters.summary:
How do regularization, nonparametric models and averaging fit the predictive view of Bayes? The chapter treats every penalty as a prior and every prior as a predictive commitment. It covers Bayesian regularization, sparse recovery and empirical Bayes (the horseshoe prior, Tweedie's formula, the lasso and global local shrinkage), discrete choice and the multinomial probit with latent utility, rare event simulation with split sampling and slice sampling, Bayesian model averaging and predictive distributions, Gaussian processes, variational inference, Bayesian additive regression trees, hierarchical models and partial pooling, Dirichlet process mixtures and clustering, and model criticism with posterior predictive checks. The common themes are the marginal likelihood as Occam's razor, shrinkage geometry with a spike for null coordinates and a tail for signals, and averaging rather than selection as the logarithmic loss optimal way to carry model uncertainty. The chapter is a survey; it catalogues no new theorem.

#### From the literature

The horseshoe estimator (Carvalho, Polson and Scott 2010); Tweedie's formula and empirical Bayes (Efron and Morris 1975); hierarchical models (Lindley and Smith 1972); multinomial probit with identified parameters (McCulloch, Polson and Rossi 2000); Bayesian additive regression trees (Chipman, George and McCulloch 2010); the Dirichlet process (Ferguson 1973); posterior predictive checks (Rubin 1984; Gelman, Meng and Stern 1996); Gaussian process regression; variational inference.

#### New results

No new results of this chapter are catalogued; the chapter is a survey of known methods.

No new results of this chapter are catalogued.

#### Key terms

chapters.title: Growth, Filtering, and Monte Carlo
chapters.summary:
How does the predictive distribution drive action and dynamic estimation over time? The chapter takes growth optimal prediction, the Kelly criterion and its portfolio form, as the case where the predictive translates directly into betting, with growth rate equal to relative entropy and side information worth mutual information. Cover's universal portfolio is then shown to be a Bayes rule: wealth is the marginal likelihood, regret is a log Bayes factor and Bayesian redundancy, and its asymptotic regret expansion matches the Rissanen and Shtarkov stochastic complexity, with worked examples on Parrondo, roulette and market data. The chapter then treats nonlinear state space models and Bayesian filtering, Hamiltonian and Langevin Monte Carlo, and particle MCMC with SMC squared and pseudo marginal methods. The recurring point is that filtering is prediction run forward and Monte Carlo makes the recursion executable.

#### From the literature

The Kelly criterion (Kelly 1956; Thorp 2006); growth optimal portfolios (Breiman 1961; Algoet and Cover 1988); Cover's universal portfolio (Cover 1991) and its regret bound with the Dirichlet one half prior (Cover and Ordentlich 1996); minimax redundancy and the Jeffreys prior (Clarke and Barron 1990, 1994); the Krichevsky and Trofimov estimator (1981); stochastic complexity (Shtarkov 1987; Rissanen 1996); Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Duane et al. 1987; Neal 2011); the no U turn sampler (Hoffman and Gelman 2014); the pseudo marginal principle (Andrieu and Roberts 2009); particle MCMC (Andrieu, Doucet and Holenstein 2010).

#### New results

The catalogued result is the Jeffreys prior equalizer for the regret of the universal portfolio; the wealth identity and the regret bound it reads as evidence and Bayesian redundancy are Cover's (1991) and Cover and Ordentlich's (1996).

- [The Jeffreys prior equalizes the regret of the universal portfolio](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#jeffreys_prior_equalizes_universal_portfolio_regret) (Theorem 10.10, page 349; conditional on the Laplace expansion of the mixture wealth, which the book states without a formal proof): In a stationary ergodic market the regret of the Bayes universal portfolio has a Laplace expansion of the Rissanen and Shtarkov type, and under the Jeffreys prior of a market family indexed by its growth optimal portfolio the constant does not depend on that portfolio, the equalizer property of Clarke and Barron carried to portfolios; the book states this without a formal proof, and for the uniform prior the first expansion recovers Cover (1991). First stated in Polson (2026), A Bayesian Interpretation of Cover's Universal Portfolio, submitted to Entropy.

#### Key terms

chapters.title: Sequential Decisions and Reinforcement Learning
chapters.summary:
How should a Bayesian choose actions when the actions change the data? The chapter treats sequential design and reinforcement learning with the predictive distribution as both guide and consequence of exploration. It covers Bayesian optimization with Gaussian process surrogates and expected improvement, Thompson sampling and Bayesian bandits with regret bounds, reinforcement learning and control as inference (KL regularized control, soft Q learning, Gibbs optimal policies), and approximate Bayesian computation (ABC, likelihood free inference) for simulators whose likelihood cannot be evaluated. The moderate deviation scale returns as the threshold behind the regret bounds, tying the decision problems to the testing and shrinkage boundaries of earlier chapters. The chapter is a survey in the book's predictive language and catalogues no new theorem.

#### From the literature

Expected improvement and efficient global optimization (Jones, Schonlau and Welch 1998); Thompson sampling (Thompson 1933) and its regret analysis (Agrawal and Goyal 2012; Russo and Van Roy 2014); control as inference and KL regularized control (Todorov 2009; Kappen 2005; Levine 2018); approximate Bayesian computation (Beaumont, Zhang and Balding 2002; Marin et al. 2012).

#### New results

No new results of this chapter are catalogued; the chapter is a survey of known methods.

No new results of this chapter are catalogued.

chapters.title: Causal Machine Learning
chapters.summary:
How can causal effects and decisions be estimated reliably when flexible machine learning supplies the nuisance fits, labels are scarce, and likelihoods are intractable? Double machine learning (DML) uses Neyman orthogonal scores and cross fitting to estimate a structural effect at the root n rate despite slow nuisance learners. Prediction powered inference (PPI) combines a small labeled sample with a large unlabeled pool through a generalized control variate (GCV) estimator, which unifies Bayes linear adjusted expectation, cross prediction powered inference and inverse probability weighted PPI, and links to the Berliner and Hill survival estimator and martingale posteriors. Generative Bayesian computation (GBC) learns a quantile neural network transport map from prior simulations to the posterior for density free inference on treatment effects and utility based policies; several of its proofs are sketches resting on assumed Bernstein and von Mises expansions. A closing discussion builds the method of types e value from Sanov's theorem.

#### From the literature

- Double machine learning with Neyman orthogonal scores and cross fitting (Chernozhukov et al. 2018; Neyman 1959).
- Cross prediction powered inference (Zrnic and Candes 2024); prediction powered inference (Angelopoulos et al. 2023).
- No semi supervised gain for a correctly specified linear model (Chakrabortty and Cai 2018), and the augmented inverse probability weighted estimator with its double robustness (Robins, Rotnitzky and Zhao 1994).
- The Horvitz and Thompson estimator (1952), Kaplan and Meier estimation (1958), inverse probability of censoring weighting (Robins and Rotnitzky 1992).
- Hill's A(n) rule (Hill 1968, 1988), the Berliner and Hill survival estimator (1988), conditionally identically distributed sequences (Berti, Pratelli and Rigo 2004) and martingale posteriors (Fong, Holmes and Walker 2023).
- Brenier's optimal transport map (Brenier 1991), implicit quantile networks (Dabney et al. 2018), and the efficiency bound for the average treatment effect (Chamberlain 1987; Hahn 1998; Hirano, Imbens and Ridder 2003).

#### New results

The control variate unification, the gain on residual reading and the Berliner and Hill limit come from the PPI paper, the quantile network consistency, efficiency and policy contraction results from the GBC paper, and the method of types e value from the paper on e values and Sanov's theorem.

- [Generalized control variate estimator, optimal shrinkage and variance](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#generalized_control_variate_unification) (Theorem 12.6, page 394; proved): The estimators of Bayes linear, cross prediction powered inference and inverse probability weighted prediction powered inference are all a baseline plus a shrunken labeled data rectifier, and the best shrinkage is a covariance over variance ratio. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026f), Linear Bayes Methods for Prediction-Powered Inference, SSRN 6744239.
- [Bayes linear and cross prediction powered inference as gain on residual updates](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#bl_and_cross_ppi_gain_on_residual) (Theorem 12.10, page 397; proved): Bayes linear and cross prediction powered inference are both a starting point plus a gain times a labeled residual, and they differ only in the gain, which for Cross PPI ignores the labeled data precision. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026f), Linear Bayes Methods for Prediction-Powered Inference, SSRN 6744239.
- [Uniform A_(n) predictive rule is conditionally identically distributed with martingale posterior CDF](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#uniform_a_n_rule_is_cid_martingale_posterior_cdf) (Theorem 12.17, page 401; proved): Hill's uniform predictive rule is a conditionally identically distributed sequence, and the martingale posterior mean of the distribution function is the empirical count over n plus one. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026f), Linear Bayes Methods for Prediction-Powered Inference, SSRN 6744239.
- [Berliner and Hill survival estimator as a limit of Bayes linear adjusted expectations](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#berliner_hill_limit_of_bayes_linear) (Theorem 12.18, page 402; proved): The Berliner and Hill survival estimator is the Kaplan and Meier product with one extra virtual observation per risk set, a limit of Bayes linear estimates and, without censoring, a martingale posterior mean. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026f), Linear Bayes Methods for Prediction-Powered Inference, SSRN 6744239.
- [Wasserstein consistency of the quantile neural network posterior](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#qnn_posterior_wasserstein_consistency) (Theorem 12.30, page 413; proved): For a scalar parameter, the posterior obtained by pushing uniform draws through a trained quantile network is within its integrated quantile error plus the sufficiency gap of the summary statistic of the exact posterior in Wasserstein distance, so it converges when both errors vanish. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026), Generative Bayesian Computation: A Measure-Theoretic Framework for Utility-Based Causal Inference, working paper.
- [Efficiency of the GBC average treatment effect estimator in a parametric structural causal model](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#gbc_ate_parametric_efficiency) (Theorem 12.35, page 415; proved): In a correctly specified parametric structural causal model, the average of the treatment effect over GBC posterior draws is asymptotically normal with the parametric information bound as variance, which never exceeds the nonparametric efficiency bound and equals it only when the efficient influence function lies in the span of the model scores. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026), Generative Bayesian Computation: A Measure-Theoretic Framework for Utility-Based Causal Inference, working paper.
- [Posterior contraction of the GBC maximum expected utility policy](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#gbc_meu_policy_posterior_contraction) (Theorem 12.41, page 421; proved): Under a Lipschitz utility, posterior contraction at a rate and a quadratic margin condition, the policy that maximizes posterior expected utility converges in mean square to the oracle policy at a rate proportional to the contraction rate, so at rate N to the minus one quarter in parametric models. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026), Generative Bayesian Computation: A Measure-Theoretic Framework for Utility-Based Causal Inference, working paper.
- [Bayes regret of the GBC maximum expected utility policy](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#gbc_meu_bayes_regret) (Corollary 12.42, page 422; proved): Without any margin condition, the expected utility lost by the policy that maximizes posterior expected utility, relative to the oracle policy, is of the order of the posterior contraction rate, so of order one over root N in parametric models. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026), Generative Bayesian Computation: A Measure-Theoretic Framework for Utility-Based Causal Inference, working paper.
- [Method of types e value with Kullback Leibler growth rate](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#method_of_types_e_value) (Theorem 12.53, page 430; proved): Dividing the maximum likelihood ratio against a simple null on a finite alphabet by a polynomial bound on the number of types gives a valid e value, whose logarithm grows at the Kullback Leibler divergence of the true law from the null. First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026), E-Values and Sanov's Theorem, working paper.

#### Key terms

chapters.title: Applications, Worked Examples, and Federated Learning
chapters.summary:
What does the book's apparatus deliver when applied end to end, and how do de Finetti and Sanov license federated Bayesian learning? The chapter has five parts. Genome wide screening tests a million hypotheses with approximate Bayes factors, whose rejection boundary grows like the square root of the log of the number of tests, with the horseshoe prior and a follow up decision problem. Bayesian decision making in medicine covers diagnostic tests as likelihood ratios, treatment thresholds, decision curves, trials under skeptical and enthusiastic priors and the value of information. Twenty one vignettes apply posterior reasoning to A/B tests, hierarchical models and small area maps. Worked examples treat the thermodynamic reading of constrained conditioning (microcanonical and canonical ensembles) with Bernoulli components, a null constraint set, the Brandeis dice and Gaussian scale mixtures. The federated section shows that exchangeability of pooled client data gives a global posterior equal to a product of local experts, adds client effects, a federated evidence lower bound, Sanov style concentration and a Bernstein and von Mises limit at the centralized rate, then treats the federated horseshoe: sufficient statistics and Gaussian approximation bias.

#### From the literature

- De Finetti's theorem and the Aldous and Hoover representation for partially exchangeable arrays (Aldous 1981; Hoover 1979).
- Sanov's theorem and large deviation rates for posterior concentration (Sanov 1957).
- Federated averaging (McMahan et al. 2017).
- The horseshoe prior (Carvalho, Polson and Scott 2010) and Wakefield's approximate Bayes factor (Wakefield 2009).
- Diagnostic threshold and decision curve methods (Pauker and Kassirer 1980; Vickers and Elkin 2006), and Bayesian clinical trial design (Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Parmar 1994; Berry 2006).

#### New results

The catalogued results are the federated ones, from the federated learning paper.

- [Federated product of experts from exchangeability](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#federated_product_of_experts) (Theorem 13.2, page 473; proved): If the pooled client data are exchangeable, the global posterior is the prior times the product of the client likelihoods, equivalently a product of size weighted local pseudo posteriors. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026f), Federated Learning, de Finetti, and Sanov, working paper.
- [Federated Sanov posterior concentration at a Kullback Leibler rate](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#federated_sanov_concentration) (Theorem 13.8, page 475; proved): The federated posterior mass outside any fixed neighborhood of the truth decays exponentially at a rate given by the smallest Kullback Leibler divergence from the truth to the outside of the neighborhood. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026f), Federated Learning, de Finetti, and Sanov, working paper.
- [Federated Bernstein and von Mises theorem](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#federated_bernstein_von_mises) (Corollary 13.9, page 476; proved): The federated posterior is asymptotically normal around the federated maximum likelihood estimate with the centralized rate and variance, so nothing is lost by not pooling raw data. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026f), Federated Learning, de Finetti, and Sanov, working paper.
- [Sufficient statistics for the federated horseshoe](https://vsokolov.org/books/elements_bayes_information/results.html#federated_horseshoe_sufficient_statistics) (Theorem 13.16, page 480; proved): In the linear model each client needs to send only a vector of size d and a residual sum of squares for the server to evaluate its marginal likelihood under the horseshoe prior. First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026f), Federated Learning, de Finetti, and Sanov, working paper.

chapters.title: Exchangeability and de Finetti
chapters.summary:
This appendix is background. It reviews exchangeability and de Finetti's theorem, the starting point of the predictive approach. A sequence is exchangeable if its law is invariant under finite permutations, a weaker condition than independence and the symmetry that Bayesian modeling assumes. chapters.title: Proper Scoring Rules and Calibration
chapters.summary:
This appendix is a short reference on proper scoring rules and calibration; the substance (the Savage representation, Bregman divergences of scores, the singling out of the log score, and the calibration and sharpness decomposition) sits in the main text. chapters.title: A Gallery of Classic Bayesian Learning Examples
chapters.summary:
Appendix T is a gallery of classic Bayesian learning problems worked in the predictive spirit of the book: a prior is a bundle of imagined observations, the posterior is the arithmetic of adding real ones, and the predictive is what remains when the parameter is integrated out. It covers conjugate updating (the coin and Laplace's rule of succession, rate, normal mean, mean and variance, category probabilities, overdispersion), named puzzles (the German tank and taxicab problems, naive Bayes, A/B testing, James and Stein shrinkage with the batting averages data, the Krichevsky and Trofimov predictor), sequential prediction and coding, concentration and PAC Bayes bounds, decision problems (the newsvendor, Wald's sequential test, the secretary problem, Gittins indices), the Kalman filter and hidden Markov models, Gaussian process regression and classification, model averaging, Good and Turing, the Bayesian bootstrap, the Laplace approximation, Elo and TrueSkill, calibration, conformal prediction, Jeffreys prior and Stein's unbiased risk estimate. Each example is a small illustration of a standard method and the appendix proves no new theorem.

#### From the literature

Rule of succession (Laplace), James and Stein shrinkage (James and Stein 1961), batting averages (Efron and Morris 1975), Krichevsky and Trofimov predictor (Krichevsky and Trofimov 1981), PAC Bayes bound (McAllester 2003; Maurer 2004), Wald's sequential probability ratio test (Wald 1947), Kalman filter (Kalman 1960), optimal experimental design (Lindley 1956), Gittins index (Gittins 1979), Good and Turing estimator and its Pitman Yor reading (Pitman and Yor 1997; Favaro, Nipoti and Teh 2016), Bayesian bootstrap (Rubin 1981), probit augmentation (Albert and Chib 1993), Elo rating (Elo 1978), Jeffreys prior, Stein's unbiased risk estimate, conformal prediction.

results.name: Componentwise constrained horizon master inequality
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).
results.summary: A fixed block of coordinates drawn from a sample conditioned on a moment window is close in total variation to independent draws from the I projection, with an explicit finite sample bound with three separately controlled terms.
results.statement: Let the alphabet have k elements, let P be a law with min_x P(x)>0, and let E be a nonempty closed convex polyhedral set of laws defined by finitely many linear moment equalities and inequalities, with window E_eps obtained by relaxing each bound by eps. Let P^star be the I projection of P onto E, assume min_x P^star(x)>0, and assume strong regularity of the windowed projections, ||P^star_eps - P^star_eps'||_TV <= C_0 |eps - eps'|. Let eps_N decrease to 0 with N eps_N > c_rnd eventually, where c_rnd/N bounds the shift of each moment under rounding to a type with denominator N. Let L_{N,I,P} be the law of the coordinates X_I of an i.i.d. P sample of size N conditioned on the empirical measure lying in E_{eps_N}. Then there is C(P,E)<infinity such that for all large N, every m element index set I and every delta>0, the total variation distance between L_{N,I,P} and the m fold product of P^star is at most m delta + m(m-1)/(2N) + C(P,E)(N+1)^{2k} exp(-2N delta^2) + C_0 m eps_N.
results.label: thm:master

results.name: Tuned rate for the constrained block law
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).
results.summary: Choosing the split radius of order the square root of log N over N gives a block law rate of order m eps_N plus m sqrt(log N / N) plus m squared over N.
results.statement: Under the hypotheses of the componentwise constrained horizon master inequality, taking delta_N = sqrt((k+1) log(N+1)/N) gives, for fixed m, that the total variation distance between the constrained block law L_{N,I,P} and the m fold product of the I projection P^star is O(m eps_N + m sqrt(log N / N) + m^2/N), where k is the alphabet size and eps_N is the window width.
results.label: cor:tuning

results.name: Projected de Finetti limit
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).
results.summary: After mixing over the constraint posterior, the block laws of an exchangeable sequence conditioned on a moment event converge to an exchangeable law whose random directing measure is the I projection of the original directing measure.
results.statement: Let Pi be a prior on laws mu over a finite alphabet, let E be a closed convex set of laws given by finitely many linear moment equalities and inequalities, with window E_eps obtained by relaxing each bound by eps, and let eps_N be window widths. Let T_E(mu) be the I projection of mu onto E, the minimizer of D(Q||mu) over Q in E; let Q_{N,mu} be the law of an i.i.d. mu sequence conditioned on the empirical measure Phat_N of its first N terms lying in E_{eps_N}; and let Pi_{N,E} be the constraint posterior, proportional to P_mu(Phat_N in E_{eps_N}) Pi(d mu). Suppose (i) Pi_{N,E} converges weakly to a law Pi_E; (ii) T_E is continuous on a neighborhood of the support of Pi_E; and (iii) for every fixed m, the Pi_{N,E}-average of the total variation distance between Q_{N,mu}(X_{1:m} in .) and T_E(mu)^{otimes m} tends to 0. Then for every fixed m and every sequence of m element index sets I_N, the law of X_{I_N} under the mixture of the Q_{N,mu} over Pi_{N,E} converges in total variation to the integral of T_E(mu)^{otimes m} against Pi_E(d mu). With Pitilde_E the pushforward of Pi_E under T_E, the laws given by the integrals of q^{otimes m} against Pitilde_E(dq) are projectively consistent and define an infinite exchangeable law whose random directing measure is Q^star = T_E(mu) with mu distributed as Pi_E.
results.label: thm:projected

results.name: Bayesian prediction under the constrained limit
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).
results.summary: Under the projected de Finetti limit, the predictive probability of the next observation is the usual de Finetti posterior predictive under the prior induced by the I projection map.
results.statement: Let Pi_E be a law on laws mu over a finite alphabet (in the projected de Finetti limit, the weak limit of the constraint posterior), let P^star_mu be the I projection of mu onto a closed convex constraint set E, and let Ptilde_E be the infinite exchangeable law whose random directing measure is Q^star = P^star_mu with mu distributed as Pi_E. For fixed t and a history x_1, ..., x_t of positive probability under Ptilde_E, Ptilde_E(X_{t+1} = x | X_{1:t} = x_{1:t}) equals the integral of P^star_mu(x) prod_{j<=t} P^star_mu(x_j) against Pi_E(d mu) divided by the integral of prod_{j<=t} P^star_mu(x_j) against Pi_E(d mu). This is the standard de Finetti posterior predictive under the induced prior, the pushforward of Pi_E under mu -> P^star_mu, and Ptilde_E(X_{t+1} in . | X_{1:t}) converges almost surely to Q^star.
results.label: cor:predict

results.name: Reachability and degeneracy of moment constraints
results.status_text: conditional on proofs of its four clauses, which the book states without proof, in particular the concentration rate max(eps_N, N^{-1/2}) and the disintegration limit in clause (ii) and the transverse dimension k-1-r_0 in clause (iv)
results.conditions: proofs of its four clauses, which the book states without proof, in particular the concentration rate max(eps_N, N^{-1/2}) and the disintegration limit in clause (ii) and the transverse dimension k-1-r_0 in clause (iv)
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).
results.summary: Whether a moment constraint is reachable by the prior decides whether the I projection acts, with reachable constraints truncating or disintegrating the prior, unreachable ones leaving genuine tilts, and affine constraints able to collapse the randomness; the book states this without proof.
results.statement: Let Pi be a prior on laws mu over a finite alphabet with k elements, let E be the polyhedral set of laws Q with <g_j,Q> = alpha_j for j <= r_0 and <g_j,Q> >= alpha_j for r_0 < j <= r, let E_eps be its window obtained by relaxing each bound by eps, let E_N be the event that the empirical measure Phat_N of N observations lies in E_{eps_N}, let Pi_{N,E}(d mu) be proportional to P_mu(E_N) Pi(d mu) (the constraint posterior), let Pi_E be its weak limit, let T_E(mu) be the I projection of mu onto E, and let I_E(mu) = inf over Q in E of D(Q||mu), which vanishes exactly on E. Pointwise in mu, (1/N) log P_mu(E_N) tends to -I_E(mu), so Pi_{N,E}(d mu) is proportional to exp(-N I_E(mu) + o_mu(N)) Pi(d mu). (i) If Pi(E) > 0 and Pi assigns zero mass to the boundary of E in the simplex, then Pi_E is Pi conditioned on E and T_E is the identity on E. (ii) If Pi(E) = 0 but E meets the support of Pi, then Pi_{N,E} concentrates on E at rate max(eps_N, N^{-1/2}), Pi_E is the disintegration of Pi along the moment map at alpha, and T_E is the identity on E. (iii) If I^star = inf over the support of Pi of I_E is positive, then Pi_{N,E} concentrates on the set where I_E = I^star and the surviving components are genuine tilts. (iv) For affine E with r_0 equality constraints, T_E(mu) = T_E(nu) if and only if mu and nu lie in a common orbit of the exponential family generated by g_1, ..., g_{r_0}, and the surviving randomness is the component of Pi_E transverse to the tilt family, of dimension k-1-r_0.
results.label: prop:reach

results.name: Decomposition of nonparametric predictive Bayes risk into Sanov and contraction terms
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026i), Nonparametric Predictive Bayes Risk, working paper.
results.summary: The predictive KL Bayes risk splits into a population Sanov term, a posterior contraction term and a small cross term, so misspecified models have risk equal to the Sanov term and well specified ones have risk equal to the contraction term.
results.statement: Let P_0 be a law on [0,1] with Lebesgue density p_0 satisfying 0 < c_0 <= p_0 <= C_0 < infinity and log p_0 in the Holder class H^beta(L) for some beta in (0, B] and L < infinity. Let the prior Pi have convex, Kullback Leibler closed support on which P -> D(P_0 || P) attains its infimum at a unique element Pi^* P_0 (the reverse I projection), whose density pi^* satisfies c_0 <= pi^* <= C_0. Assume Hellinger contraction: for some epsilon_n -> 0 with n epsilon_n^2 -> infinity and constants M, c > 0, the posterior mass of { P : d_H(P, Pi^* P_0) > M epsilon_n } is at most exp(-c n epsilon_n^2) in P_0^{\otimes n} probability, where d_H^2(P, Q) = (1/2) integral (sqrt p - sqrt q)^2 dx. Assume the Wong and Shen condition: there are eta > 0, M_WS >= 1 and C_WS < infinity with D(pi^* || p) <= C_WS d_H(P, Pi^* P_0)^2 whenever d_H(P, Pi^* P_0) <= eta and pi^* <= M_WS p. Let hat p_Pi be the posterior predictive density, R_KL(P_0; hat p_Pi) = E_{P_0^{\otimes n}} D(p_0 || hat p_Pi) and J_n(Pi, P_0) = E_{P_0^{\otimes n}} D(Pi^* P_0 || hat p_Pi). Then R_KL(P_0; hat p_Pi) = D(P_0 || Pi^* P_0) + J_n(Pi, P_0) + r_n, where |r_n| <= C ( sqrt(D(P_0 || Pi^* P_0) J_n(Pi, P_0)) + J_n(Pi, P_0) ) with C = e C_0 / c_0. If J_n -> 0 and D(P_0 || Pi^* P_0) > 0 then R_KL = D(P_0 || Pi^* P_0)(1 + o(1)); if D(P_0 || Pi^* P_0) = 0 then R_KL = J_n(Pi, P_0)(1 + o(1)).
results.label: np:thm:abc-csiszar

results.name: Conditional Sanov and tilted de Finetti
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2025a), De Finetti + Sanov = Bayes: Forward and Inverse Sanov in Bayesian Prediction, Statistical Science (revised short communication).
results.summary: Conditioned on the empirical measure lying in a closed convex set, the predictive law of a fixed block converges to the I projection of the de Finetti baseline onto that set.
results.statement: Let (X_i) be infinitely exchangeable with de Finetti mixing measure Pi, and let E be a closed convex subset of the probability measures with inf over P in E of D(P || Pi^dagger) finite, for a de Finetti baseline Pi^dagger. Conditional on the event that the empirical measure of X_1, ..., X_n lies in E, the predictive law of any fixed block of size m converges to P^circ = argmin over P in E of D(P || Pi^dagger), at rate O(m / n^{1/3}).
results.label: np:thm:tilted

results.name: Bayes risk optimal Kolmogorov Smirnov threshold at the moderate deviation scale
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026b), Bayes Risk for Goodness of Fit Tests.
results.summary: The Bayes risk optimal Kolmogorov Smirnov threshold sits at about half the detection distance, with the exact constant 3/8 and risk of order n to the minus 25/16 at the boundary Delta_n = sqrt(2 log n) with prior odds n.
results.statement: For the Kolmogorov Smirnov test of the book with Type I error given by Kolmogorov's tail and Type II error equal to the stated bound on the Pitman family with detection scale Delta_n, and prior odds b_n = pi_1 / pi_0, the unique Bayes risk minimizing threshold is c_n^* = Delta_n / 2 - (log b_n) / (4 Delta_n) (1 + o(1)). In the interior regime log b_n = o(Delta_n^2), c_n^* = (1/2) Delta_n (1 + o(1)) and the minimum Bayes risk is B_n(c_n^*) = 4 pi_0 sqrt(b_n) exp( -Delta_n^2 / 2 - (log b_n)^2 / (8 Delta_n^2) ) (1 + o(1)) = O( b_n^{-1/2} e^{-Delta_n^2/2} ). At the boundary Delta_n = sqrt(2 log n), b_n = n, one has c_n^* = (3/8) Delta_n (1 + o(1)) and B_n(c_n^*) = Theta(n^{-25/16}).
results.label: np:thm:rs

results.name: General moderate deviation risk balancing threshold for tests
results.origin_text: First stated in Datta, Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi (2026), A New Look at Bayesian Testing.
results.summary: For any statistic with Gaussian type moderate deviation tails under null and alternative, the Bayes risk optimal threshold is half the detection scale plus a prior odds correction, and it is at least the multiple comparison scale sqrt(2 log b_n).
results.statement: Let T_n / sigma_n converge in law to a nondegenerate limit Z, and let the alternatives sit at detection scale Delta_n -> infinity with P_0(T_n > a sigma_n) = exp(-a^2/2 + o(Delta_n^2)) and P_1(T_n <= a sigma_n) = exp(-(Delta_n - a)^2/2 + o(Delta_n^2)) uniformly in 0 < a < Delta_n. For the Bayes risk R_n(a) = pi_0 P_0(T_n > a sigma_n) + pi_1 P_1(T_n <= a sigma_n) with log(pi_0 / pi_1) / Delta_n^2 -> lambda in (-1/2, 1/2), every Bayes risk minimizing threshold satisfies a_n^* = ( Delta_n / 2 + log(pi_0/pi_1) / Delta_n )(1 + o(1)) and R_n(a_n^*) = pi_0 exp( -(a_n^*)^2/2 + o(Delta_n^2) ). When pi_0 / pi_1 = b_n >= 1, a_n^* >= sqrt(2 log b_n) (1 + o(1)) and R_n(a_n^*) <= pi_1 < 1 / b_n.
results.label: np:thm:rs-general

results.name: Optimal truncation at the moderate deviation scale
results.origin_text: New in this book.
results.summary: The book conjectures that the Bayes risk optimal truncation level for a Kolmogorov Smirnov truncated predictive density equals the detection distance, which is sqrt(2 log n) at the detection boundary, and gives a heuristic only.
results.statement: Under the density, Holder, convex support, Hellinger contraction and Wong and Shen assumptions of the predictive Bayes risk decomposition (a density p_0 bounded away from 0 and infinity with log p_0 Holder, a prior with convex Kullback Leibler closed support and reverse I projection Pi^* P_0 with density bounded above and below, Hellinger contraction at rate epsilon_n, and the Wong and Shen condition), let P_0 (possibly depending on n) have CDF F_{P_0} and let Delta_n = sqrt(n) sup_x |F_{P_0}(x) - F_Pi^*(x)|, where F_Pi^* is the CDF of the reverse I projection Pi^* P_0. If Delta_n -> infinity and h_n Delta_n^2 -> infinity, then the Bayes risk optimal truncation level a_n^* of the truncated predictive density of the book satisfies a_n^* = Delta_n (1 + o(1)). In particular at Delta_n = sqrt(2 log n) with h_n log n -> infinity, a_n^* = sqrt(2 log n) (1 + o(1)).
results.label: np:conj:ks-mdp

results.name: Master decomposition and the contraction term rate
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026i), Nonparametric Predictive Bayes Risk, working paper.
results.summary: Hellinger posterior contraction at rate epsilon_n gives a contraction term of order epsilon_n squared in the predictive risk decomposition, via the Wong and Shen conversion of Hellinger to KL.
results.statement: Under the assumptions of the predictive Bayes risk decomposition (a density p_0 bounded away from 0 and infinity with log p_0 Holder, a prior with convex Kullback Leibler closed support and reverse I projection Pi^* P_0 with density pi^* bounded above and below, and Hellinger contraction at rate epsilon_n), let U_n = { P : d_H(P, Pi^* P_0) <= M epsilon_n and pi^* <= M_WS p }, with epsilon_n the Hellinger contraction rate and M_WS the Wong and Shen constant. If E_{P_0^{\otimes n}} of the posterior integral over the complement of U_n of D(pi^* || p) is O(epsilon_n^2), then J_n(Pi, P_0) = O(epsilon_n^2). For a prior adapting over a grid of size b_n, epsilon_n is the contraction rate of the adaptive posterior.
results.label: np:thm:master

results.name: Adaptive Dirichlet process mixture predictive rate

results.conditions: the data driven bandwidth stays within constant factors of the optimal bandwidth, which the book assumes and does not prove
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026i), Nonparametric Predictive Bayes Risk, working paper.
results.summary: A Dirichlet process mixture of Gaussians attains the near minimax predictive KL rate for Holder smooth densities with a log n factor, given a sketch proof that assumes the bandwidth stays near its optimum.
results.statement: For a density p_0 in the Holder class H^beta(L) with beta in (0, B] unknown, if the data driven bandwidth of the Dirichlet process mixture of Gaussians stays within constant factors of h_n^* = n^{-1/(2 beta + 1)}, then J_n(DPM, P_0) is bounded above, up to a constant, by n^{-2 beta/(2 beta + 1)} log n.

results.status_text: conditional on the marginal likelihood truncation level stays within O(1) of the optimal level, which the book assumes and does not prove
results.conditions: the marginal likelihood truncation level stays within O(1) of the optimal level, which the book assumes and does not prove
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Zantedeschi (2026i), Nonparametric Predictive Bayes Risk, working paper.
results.summary: A canonical Polya tree attains the predictive KL rate n to the minus 2 beta over 2 beta plus 1 up to a log n factor for smoothness below one, given a sketch proof that assumes the selected level is near optimal.
results.statement: For p_0 in the Holder class H^beta(L) with beta in (0, 1) unknown, if the marginal likelihood truncation level of the canonical Polya tree stays within O(1) of L_n^* = (log_2 n) / (2 beta + 1), then J_n(PT, P_0) is bounded above, up to a constant, by n^{-2 beta/(2 beta + 1)} log n.

results.name: Adaptive logistic Gaussian process predictive rate
results.status_text: conditional on the posterior contracts in Hellinger at the rate that van der Vaart and van Zanten (2009) prove for the squared exponential kernel; the remaining hypotheses of the master decomposition theorem (its density and Wong and Shen assumptions and its tail condition, that the posterior expected divergence D(pi^* || p) over laws P with d_H(P, Pi^* P_0) > M epsilon_n or pi^* > M_WS p is O(epsilon_n^2)), which the book assumes and does not check for this prior
results.conditions: the posterior contracts in Hellinger at the rate that van der Vaart and van Zanten (2009) prove for the squared exponential kernel; the remaining hypotheses of the master decomposition theorem (its density and Wong and Shen assumptions and its tail condition, that the posterior expected divergence D(pi^* || p) over laws P with d_H(P, Pi^* P_0) > M epsilon_n or pi^* > M_WS p is O(epsilon_n^2)), which the book assumes and does not check for this prior
